title: Bright liver, body composition and insulin resistance changes with nutritional intervention: a follow-up study.
source_type: Liver international : official journal of the International Association for the Study of the Liver
text_summary: 本随访研究纳入50名超重NAFLD患者，实施6个月适度低热量、均衡饮食和生活方式干预，并比较超声亮肝评分、体重、体成分及胰岛素抵抗。干预后亮肝评分、体重、BMI、HOMA-IR及多项肝脏超声尺寸和生化指标显著下降；基线HOMA-IR可解释部分亮肝程度，干预后的亮肝变化主要由体重和肝纵径变化预测。结果支持超声亮肝评分联合体重和肝脏测量作为营养干预后临床代谢改善的实用指标。

CLINICAL STUDIES
Bright liver , body composition and insulin resistance changes with
nutritional intervention: a follow-up study
Daniela Catalano, Guglielmo M. Trovato, Giuseppe F . Martines, Marianna Randazzo and
Antonia Tonzuso
Dipartimento di Medicina Interna, Istituto di Medicina Interna e Terapia Medica, Facolta` di Medicina e Chirurgia, Universita` di Catania, Catania, Italia
Keywords
body composition – bright liver – diet – insulin
resistance – NAFLD – nutrition – steatosis –
ultrasound
Correspondence
Daniela Catalano, MD, Dipartimento di
Medicina Interna, Istituto di Medicina Interna e
Terapia Medica, Facolta` di Medicina e Chirurgia,
Universita` di Catania, Via Sant’Orsola 30,
95131, Catania, Italia
Tel: 139 3477379383/139 3358364356
Fax 139 095 317349
e-mail: danielacatalano@unict.it
Received 21 December 2007
Accepted 24 February 2008
DOI:10.1111/j.1478-3231.2008.01742.x
Abstract
Background: Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) because of its association
with obesity, diabetes and insulin resistance (IR), is the hepatic expression of
metabolic syndrome. Exercise and nutritional intervention can improve and
prevent these inter-related conditions; the relationships between the degree of IR
and ultrasound (US) morphological post-interventional changes are not deﬁned.
Aims: The aim of our study was to assess the relationship, if any, in NAFLD
patients, among IR, BMI and degree of bright liver, before and after 6 months of a
moderately hypocaloric/balanced dietary/lifestyle treatment. Fifty outpatients with
a clinical and US diagnosis of NAFLD were studied. Methods: Liver echogenicity
[Bright Liver Score (BLS)] was scored on a four-graded scale. IR was assessed by
homoeostasis model-insulin resistance (HOMA-IR). Body composition was
assessed by bioimpedance assessment and skinfold measurements. Results: A
signiﬁcant decrease of BLS was observed, with a concurrent decrease of body
weight, body mass index (BMI) and HOMA-IR. Bright liver decrease has a trend
parallel to IR, much less steep than the trend of bright liver reduction against US
liver dimensions, body weight and BMI decrease. HOMA-IR is the only baseline
variable that enters signiﬁcantly in the multiple regression and, alone, explains
21.4% of variance in predicting bright liver degree. After dietary interventions,
both HOMA-IR and BMI are signiﬁcantly involved in the multiple regression and
explain, together, 42.3% of variance in predicting bright liver degree; variation in
BLS can be predicted by variation of body weight and of US longitudinal
measurement of the liver. Conclusions: Liver US BLS appears to be a useful tool,
both alone and along with other US measurements and body weight changes, for
the assessment of clinical-metabolic amelioration in patients treated with dietetic
interventions. The clinical-diagnostic role, if any, of other assessed laboratory
analyses, in the subset of NAFLD, does not appear to be deﬁnite.
Fatty liver is generally described as a condition with
accumulation of triglycerides and other fats in liver
cells and, when not associated with alcohol assump-
tion and without histological and/or serological signs
of inﬂammation, is called nonalcoholic fatty liver
disease (NAFLD) (1, 2). NAFLD is associated with an
increased risk of all-cause death, probably because of
complications of insulin resistance (IR) such as vascu-
lar disease (3). Metabolic syndrome, which can be
linked to type II diabetes, obesity and/or hypertrigly-
ceridaemia and other factors (4), is most commonly
associated with fatty liver.
Although liver biopsy is still the gold standard, liver
ultrasound (US) is a useful tool in clinical practice and
epidemiological studies, used widely also for logistic
and ethical reasons. In addition, liver US has a good
correlation with the histological ﬁndings of fatty
inﬁltration (5, 6), despite the fact that US is very much
an operator-dependent procedure, and that there
could be a problem when trying to extrapolate data
to other centres. Both standardization of criteria and
minimizing interobserver variations are useful for
performing longitudinal studies more reliably.
Although NAFLD is known to also occur in lean
individuals, which indicates that excessive adiposity
is not required for the development of NAFLD, IR
and severity of NAFLD tend to parallel each other
and obesity itself, when present (7). However, the

multifactorial natural history of NAFLD in a commu-
nity remains substantially controversial (8). Assess-
ment of liver echogenicity is of value for detection or
exclusion of moderate to pronounced fatty inﬁltra-
tion, but cannot be relied upon in diagnosing ﬁbrosis
in asymptomatic patients with mild to moderately
elevated liver transaminases (9–11). Moreover, it was
reported that fatty liver is also associated with an
impaired hepatic blood ﬂow characterized by increased
intrahepatic resistances; these vascular changes could
be reversed by dietary and metformin treatment (12).
Bright liver echo pattern is a sign of liver steatosis of
good sensitivity and speciﬁcity, and liver ﬁbrosis does
not interfere critically with US measurements (13).
There is no precise consent on the effects and
features of an optimal nutritional strategy in NAFLD.
Lifestyle modiﬁcations, including dietary change and
increased exercise aimed to promote weight loss, are
currently considered to be beneﬁcial (14). This can be
done even through quite moderate weight loss,
achieved by dietary restriction, either alone (15, 16),
in combination with exercise (17) or using a pharma-
cological intervention (18, 19). However, the nature
and rapidity of weight loss has been shown to be
important (20) but not clearly beneﬁcial. Moderate
amounts of weight loss as well as exercise induce a
decrease of IR, and are currently regarded as the
correct therapeutic strategy for patients with NAFLD
who are overweight or obese (21–23). Liver biochem-
istry [alanine aminotransferase (AL T)] and hepatic
steatosis share improvement with dietary treatment
(20) but hepatic inﬂammation and ﬁbrosis are not
modiﬁed, when present. Even if a caloric constraint to
25–30 kcal/kg/day is commonly considered to be ap-
propriate to reach approximately 10% of body weight
decrease over 6 months, the most advantageous nutri-
tional approach to manage NAFLD has not yet been
deﬁned (24, 25). Most trials have used a balanced diet
with caloric restriction, but a lower carbohydrate diet
is associated with lower post-interventional serum
levels of triglyceride and higher high-density lipopro-
tein (HDL) cholesterol levels (26).
The aim of our study was to investigate whether the
effects of nutritional interventions that we currently
recommend have an effect on the degree of bright liver
assessed by US.
The secondary outcome was to evaluate whether the
degree of bright liver and its changes can be predicted
by baseline and/or the ﬁnal nutritional/laboratory
measurements (such as AL T, insulin, body weight and
body composition), and to which extent these are
related to diet adherence, as measured by body weight
decrease.
Patients and methods
Fifty outpatients with a clinical and US diagnosis of
Bright Liver were studied consecutively from January
2005 to February 2007 at the Internal Medicine Day-
Hospital of the University Hospital of Catania (Italy).
The criteria of NAFLD were: (a) absolutely negative
history of alcohol consumption from at least 5 years;
exclusion of other chronic liver diseases (hepatitis B,
hepatitis C, genetic haemochromatosis and auto-
immune conditions, drug use, haemoglobinopathy)
and (b) US bright liver pattern, assumed to be
evidence of hepatic steatosis. Body mass index was
evaluated according to the World Health Organization
(WHO) criteria (1997). Weight was measured in light
clothing, without shoes, in kg and height was mea-
sured in centimetres, using a scale-integrated stadi-
ometer. Bioimpedance assessment (BIA) of body
composition was performed by a single-frequency
BIA device 50 kHz and 800 mA (model BIA 101 RJL;
Akern, Firenze, Italy) according to the standard tetra-
polar technique; to avoid artefacts, the electrodes were
placed on the feet, ankles, hands and wrists. The body
composition was calculated from BIA measurements
(resistance and reactance) and anthropometric vari-
ables [Body Weight (BW) and Height (H)], using the
software provided by the Akern/RJL Systems. This
predictive model allows for calculation of total body
water (TBW), body fat mass (BIA-FM) and fat-free
mass (BIA-FFM), body cell mass (BCM) and extra-
cellular water (ECW); all measurements are expressed
in kg and in relative percentages (27).
Body mass index was calculated as BW/H
2 and
patients were categorized as normal weight
(o25.0 kg/m
2), overweight ( Z25.0 and /C2029.9 kg/
m2) and obese ( Z30.0 kg/m2). The obesity was classi-
ﬁed into grade I (30.0–34.9 kg/m 2), grade II
(35.0–39.9 kg/m2) and grade III ( Z40.0 kg/m2). Pa-
tients with any history of diabetes mellitus, established
by a fasting glucose level Z126 mg/dl or a glycated
haemoglobin level Z6.5%, or those under treatment,
were excluded from this study.
Ultrasound examination was performed by the
same most experienced echographist (to reduce
interobserver variability) unaware of clinical details
at the time of the procedure, using a GE echo-colour-
doppler equipment, (GE Logiq 5 Expert US equip-
ment, GE Medical Systems, Milwaukee, WI, USA)
high resolution, with real-time sectional scan
transducers.
The liver was assessed for size, contour, echogeni-
city, structure, penetration of the US beam, i.e.
posterior beam attenuation and portal vessel wall

Catalano et al. Bright liver and IR changes with nutritional intervention

 

distinction; these last criteria were especially assessed
in the report of the degree of steatosis.
The degrees of bright liver considered for statistical
evaluation were classiﬁed unifying three subscales
focused on echogenicity, beam penetration and portal
vessel wall distinction (9):
Grade 0: normal or slightly reduced in comparison
with right kidney echogenicity;
Grade 1: slightly increased in comparison with right
kidney echogenicity;
Grade 2 : clearly increased, with a fall in echo
amplitude (i.e. posterior beam attenuation owing to
the high reﬂectivity of the fat liver parenchyma); and
Grade 3 : markedly increased with a fall in echo
amplitude and impaired portal vessel wall distinction,
i.e. loss of echoes from the walls of the portal vein.
Clinical physical examination and routine labora-
tory measurements were performed. These include
virus hepatitis (HA V , HBV and HCV) and cancer
markers (AFP , CEA, Ca- 125, Ca 15-3), fT3, fT4,
TSH, PTH, aspartate aminotransferase (AST), AL T,
g-glutamyl transpeptidase ( g-GT), total protein and
albumin. Participants were in sinus rhythm, with
normal EKG and without known ischaemic heart
disease. Blood pressure was measured using a mercury
sphygmomanometer in three positions (supine, sitting
and standing) after a 15-min rest. Arterial hyperten-
sion was deﬁned as 4 140 mmHg of systolic and
4 90 mmHg of diastolic blood pressure. Moreover,
hypertension levels were divided into categories of
mild, moderate and severe (renamed stages 1, 2 and 3
respectively), according to the Joint National Com-
mittee on Detection, Evaluation and Treatment of
High Blood Pressure (28).
Insulin resistance was assessed by homoeostasis
model-insulin resistance index (HOMA-IR) (29),
according to the following formulas: HOMA-IR (30)
was calculated using the formula ‘fasting insulin value
/C2fasting blood sugar level/405, equivalent to the
HOMA-formula: HOMA = fasting serum insulin
(mU/ml) /C2fasting plasma glucose ( mM/L)/22.5 (30).
HOMA correlates with the IR index measured by the
hyperinsulinaemic euglycaemic clamp method, even
though it has a suboptimal reproducibility, reﬂecting
day-to-day variability in fasting glucose and insulin
levels (30).
Patients were referred to the Internal Medicine Day
Hospital, involved in a programme of interventional
health psychology, mainly aimed at life-style modiﬁca-
tions. The aim of the treatment was a gradual weight
loss of approximately 5% of the initial body weight
within 6 months in obese overweight subjects. How-
ever, the key goal of the diet was to achieve an adequate
nutritional status, with a close reference to daily
physical activity and to the degree of weight abnorm-
ality, in order to prevent malnutrition-related liver
degenerative progression. Personalized low-lipid diets
were allowed, with daily recommendations derived
also from the software used (Dietosystem
TM, Milan,
Italy). Subjects attended a total of seven scheduled
encounters and visits with one of the physicians for
clinical evaluation monthly.
Activity was encouraged in the form of walking
using the ‘10 000 steps a day’ suggestion, and adher-
ence and compliance were enhanced suggesting the
most appealing physical activity possibilities. W eight
modiﬁcations through the prescribed diets were fore-
seen, but without the aim of reaching rapid effects
both on weight and on liver steatosis.
A complete laboratory, instrumental (US), anthro-
pometrical and clinical reassessment was carried out
after 6 months from the beginning of this study and
follow-up.
Statistical analysis
Statistical analyses were performed using
SPSS 13.0
software package. A preliminary comparison was
performed by paired Student’s t-test on the changes
of all variables. Pearson’s or Spearman’s correlation, as
appropriate, was performed in the overall group of
patients between the degree of bright liver [Bright
Liver Score (BLS)] vs. HOMA-IR (insulin sensitivity),
demographical, metabolic and nutritional measure-
ments. Stepwise multiple regression was used to
weight the relative contribution of each of the inde-
pendent variables (baseline and final) in predicting
BLS changes. A critical P value o 0.05 was considered
to be significant.
Results
Fifty overweight, weight-stable, NAFLD patients (aged
47.1 /C613.5 years; 23 males aged 46.7 /C614.6 years and
28 females aged 47.4/C612.8 years) with BMI425 kg/m
2
entered this study. There were 24 smokers, seven of
whom had given up for at least 5 years. There was no
reported change in smoking status during this study.
According to the Mediterranean diet prescribed, the
ﬁnal post-intervention median dietary fat intake was
26.1 /C62.9%; the median carbohydrate intake was
54.7 /C63.4%; and the median dietary protein intake
was 19.1 /C61.9%. All patients, when accurately asked,
were compliant with the diet and prescriptions for
physical activity increase. However, different degrees
of body weight changes were observed in different

Bright liver and IR changes with nutritional intervention Catalano et al.

 

patients, suggesting that a nonuniform patients’ com-
pliance was achieved.
Considering all the patients, the mean baseline
BMI was 32.7 /C66.2 and it decreased to 31.7 /C66.2
(P o 0.003); the baseline mean body weight was
89.4 /C616.3 kg and it decreased to 86.6 /C616.8
(P o 0.003). The mean weight reduction over the
6-month study was close to 57.0% of the desired loss.
The prevalence and distribution according to gen-
der, age groups, educational level, coffee use and
cigarette smoking, performed by w2, did not show any
difference with regard to BMI, BLS and HOMA post-
intervention changes.
The results on the baseline and post-intervention
nutritional, laboratory and US liver measurements
values at 6 months are reported in Table 1. A paired
Student’s t-test was used for assessing signiﬁcant
differences. Considering gender, age groups, educa-
tional level, coffee use and cigarette smoking, all these
factors do not affect BMI, BLS and HOMA post-
intervention changes. Body weight and BMI decrease,
reduction of blood glucose, IR (HOMA), AL T, g-GT
and alkaline phosphatase are signiﬁcant (paired Stu-
dent’s t-test). Decrease or normalization of the BLS,
along with a decrease of liver volume and diameters,
was observed.
Univariate correlation analyses (Table 2) were
performed between the degree of bright liver (BLS)
vs. HOMA-IR (insulin sensitivity), demographical,
laboratory (insulin, blood glucose, AST, AL T, g-GT,
cholesterol total and HDL, triglycerides, alkaline phos-
phatase) and nutritional measurements (body weight,
BMI, fat mass assessed by BIA). Analyses were per-
formed using the baseline, ﬁnal values and changes of
each parameter. Variables with weak (no more than
P o 0.05) and/or absent correlations vs. BLS and
relative changes did not enter in the multiple regres-
sion analysis model. The results of stepwise multiple
regression, used to weigh the relative contribution
of each of the independent variables (baseline and
changes of HOMA-IR, triglycerides, serum enzymes,
i.e. AL T, g-GT, and alkaline phosphatase, body com-
position and of BMI) in predicting BLS changes, are
reported separately.
In baseline results, HOMA-IR is the only variable
that enters signiﬁcantly in the multiple regression and,
alone, explains 21.4% of variance in predicting bright
liver degree (Table 3).
After dietary interventions, both HOMA-IR and
BMI are signiﬁcantly involved in the multiple regres-
sion and explain, together, 42.3% of the variance in
predicting bright liver degree (Table 4).

Change of BLS is predicted by variation of body
weight and of US measurement of longitudinal dia-
meter of liver: both variables together explain 35.3% of
variance in predicting bright liver degree (Table 5).
Discussion
Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease is a common diagnosis
in clinical practice, derived both from US imaging of
bright liver and from a realistic exclusion of infective,
inﬂammatory and/or toxic causes (alcohol and drugs).
Even if it is widely accepted that IR and oxidative stress
(31) play an important role in NAFLD development
and progression, several inter-related clinical and
pathophysiological features are still quite conjectural
(31). The impact of NAFLD on health-related quality
of life is far from being deﬁned and the assumption
that preventing and/or treating the metabolic syn-
drome would prevent and/or treat NAFLD, affecting

liver-related morbidity and mortality is likely, but
widely speculative. Lifestyle intervention may improve
NAFLD, but medications that increase insulin sensi-
tivity and the antioxidant defences in the liver deserve
evaluation in carefully controlled trials (31). In most
reported trials, even with frequent dietary assessments,
a critical point is the poor compliance with an
adherence of 60–70% to dietary and lifestyle interven-
tions (16, 26). Also, in our study, as usual, patients’
compliance to dietary prescriptions is not uniform,
reaching different weight modiﬁcation. From our
results, some consideration on a dietary intervention
and on some feasible lifestyle modiﬁcation can be
drawn. No clear effect of age, gender, cigarette smok-
ing and coffee beverages habits on the presence and
modiﬁcation of bright liver is present in our patients:
hence, in a ﬁrst approach, these are not factors with a
major impact on NAFLD and, notably, the modiﬁable
factors, i.e. cigarette smoking and coffee beverages
habits, are not a primary goal for practical lifestyle
modiﬁcation in this regard.
The selected nutritional approach affected the de-
gree of bright liver assessed by US (Table 1). Along
with the decrease of the degree of bright liver, there is
on average a remarkable and signiﬁcant decrease of
liver dimension as assessed and measured by the US
equipment and, conceivably, this could also be gauged
at a physical examination (a decrease of about 1 cm in
the longitudinal dimension of the liver means that a
liver, previously detected by the hand of the physician,
thereafter is not anymore appreciated). Intrahepatic
Doppler blood ﬂows, already normal, did not show
any change.
Among nutritional and laboratory measurements,
AL T,g-GT and blood glucose showed the most im-
portant decrease, whereas blood lipids did not change
signiﬁcantly.
The patients in our study received detailed recom-
mendations on diet and daily physical activity, propo-
sals that, according to reports of individual dietary
diary, were not followed uniformly. However, even a
slight weight and BMI decrease was associated with an
improvement of US liver pattern (decrease or disap-
pearance of bright liver), and both BMI and body
weight have a close linear correlation with the decrease
of the US degree of steatosis (Table 2– BLS changes
column). It is interesting to notice that the US
measurements of liver dimensions paralleled a higher
signiﬁcant correlation improvement of BLS (Table 2).
The insulin resistance (HOMA-IR) paralleled the im-
provement in the US degree of steatosis (BLS) as g-GT
did (Table 2). AST and AL T, as expected, share a good
correlation with the degree of liver steatosis with g-GT
(Table 2– baseline, before the diet column), which is
not present anymore after the dietary intervention
(Table 2– baseline, after the diet column). Hence, g-
GT appears to be most reliable for assessing parallel
modiﬁcation of serological measurement and mor-
phological changes. The relationships between NAFLD
and transaminase were the object of several studies
(9, 32); moreover, it was reported that weight loss,
reduction of g-GT and, to a lesser extent, in AST, are
predictive of improved lobular inﬂammation and
ﬁbrosis, key prognostic features of NAFLD (20).
The degree of bright liver and its changes can be
predicted with a fair approximation by noninvasive
measurements (baseline and changes of HOMA-IR,
triglycerides, serum enzymes, i.e. AL T, g-GT and alka-
line phosphatase, body composition and of BMI).
Considering the baseline results, HOMA-IR is the only
variable that enters signiﬁcantly in the multiple regres-
sion and, alone, explains 21.4% of the variance in
predicting bright liver degree (Table 3). It suggests that
HOMA-IR is the most useful laboratory tool for
envisaging reliably the presence of bright liver as
assessed by US in patients not speciﬁcally managed
with dietary prescriptions.
In treated patients, i.e. after the adherence to a pro-
longed period of dietary prescription, both HOMA-IR
and BMI predict at about 43% the degree of bright
liver, i.e. both variables are useful in the discrimination
of liver US patterns closer to normal (Table 4).
Information and suggestion deriving from the step-
wise multiple regression analyses for the prediction of
changes in the BLS are quite different (Table 5): only
changes of body weight, in kg, and changes of the US
longitudinal measurement of the liver consistently
predict the changes, i.e. the decrease, of US-assessed
bright liver.
It is important that there was no deﬁnite cut-off of
body weight decrease at which any improvement in
bright liver, insulin sensitivity and/or serum enzymes
could be appreciated; even patients with a slight body
weight decrease showed clear clinically favourable
effects.

Reciprocally, US imaging (reduction or disappear-
ance of bright liver pattern) can be regarded as a
sensitive and independent index of adequacy and
compliance related not only to lessened caloric in-
come, as assessed by body weight decrease, but also
with some additional information on a qualitative diet
compliance deriving from the amelioration of US liver
appearance.
The extent to which the liver appearance amelio-
rates at US imaging has a parallel trend with the
decrease of IR, but the trend is much less steep in
comparison with the trend of bright liver reduction
against US liver dimensions, body weight and BMI
decrease (Table 2).
Liver US BLS seems to be a useful tool, both alone
and along with other US measurements and body
weight changes, for the assessment of clinical-meta-
bolic amelioration in patients treated with dietetic
interventions. The clinical-diagnostic role, if any, of
other assessed laboratory analyses, including IR, in the
subset of NAFLD, does not appear to be deﬁnite.

image_summary: 第1页：Liver International临床研究首页，含题名、作者、关键词、摘要和引言；评估营养干预后亮肝、体成分与胰岛素抵抗的变化。
第2页：双栏正文说明研究目的、50名亮肝患者的纳入标准、人体测量、身体成分评估和超声检查方法。
第3页：方法页定义超声亮肝0至3级、实验室指标、生活方式和低热量均衡饮食方案及统计方法，页末进入受试者随访结果。
第4页：正文报告完成干预者及体重、BMI、代谢指标变化；表1比较50名NAFLD患者干预前后的营养、生化及肝脏超声测量值。
第5页：表2列出干预前、干预后及变化量中亮肝评分与实验室、人体测量和超声指标的相关性；表3和表4给出亮肝评分的逐步多元回归模型。
第6页：表5给出亮肝评分变化的逐步回归预测因素；正文讨论体重、肝纵径、HOMA-IR和转氨酶变化与超声改善的关系。
第7页：双栏讨论结尾与结论，评价超声亮肝作为营养干预随访指标的价值与局限，随后列出参考文献1至24。
第8页：参考文献末页，列出其余引文25至32，无图表。
